prompt: Gradients of the GARCH likelihood would have to be carried back through the whole day-by-day recursion, so you choose a method that only needs the score.
trap: The likelihood is the objective; Nelder–Mead is how you search it.

prompt: With 6 parameters, the search keeps 7 points and moves the worst one each step.
why: A simplex in d dimensions has d + 1 vertices.

prompt: Each step first tries the point c + (c − x_w), mirroring the worst point through the centroid of the others.
why: That's the reflect move; expand doubles it, contract halves back, shrink pulls all points toward the best.

prompt: When reflecting and contracting both fail, every point except the best moves halfway toward the best one.
tells: every point except the best moves halfway
trap: It happens only when nothing else improves.

prompt: After converging, the search restarts from its best point with a simplex half the size, and stops when the score improves by less than 10⁻⁶.
why: Restarts guard against Nelder–Mead stalling or collapsing too early.
trap: A practical fix for the method's known weakness.

prompt: A colleague wants to use the same simplex method for a model with 300 parameters.
why: Nelder–Mead scales poorly with dimension; gradient methods (e.g. BFGS with automatic differentiation) fit large models better.
trap: Knowing where your tool stops working is part of mastering it.
